title: Paper 1 Writing Basics: Purpose, Format, Register and G.A.A.P.
summary: Everything you need before any non-fiction genre: purpose vs format, formal vs informal language, reading the task, the G.A.A.P. technique, a 5-minute plan, paragraphing and a strong sample.

blocks.text: In Checkpoint 6 Paper 1, the writing task is worth **25 marks**: half of the whole paper. Before you learn any single genre (autobiography, recount, diary, letter, review…), you need the skills on this page. You will learn **why** you are writing (purpose), **what shape** the writing must take (format), whether to sound **formal or informal** (register), how to read the task with the **G.A.A.P.** technique, how to plan in five minutes and how to build strong paragraphs. Every genre page in this course is built on these foundations, so study this page first.
1. Where the writing task sits in Paper 1

rows: Read one or more non-fiction texts and answer questions on them.
Write ONE non-fiction piece. There is space to plan before you write.
Reading and writing are in the same paper, so you must watch the clock yourself.

blocks.text: Paper 2 (Fiction) has exactly the same shape (Reading 25 + Writing 25 in 1 hour), but its writing task is a story. Recent Paper 1 writing tasks have included a **review** of a toy for a children's magazine, a **news report** for a school newspaper and a **balanced argument** about where a new recycling centre should go. Other non-fiction types from the curriculum can also appear: letters, persuasive writing, information texts, instructions, recounts, diaries, biographies and articles. That is why this course gives you a pack for every genre.
How your writing is marked (out of 25)

rows: Are the ideas relevant and developed? Is the writing right for the purpose, the reader and the text type? Does it keep the reader interested?
Are the words chosen carefully, for this text type and for effect?
Structure of texts (the teacher's older name: Text structure)
Is it well organised: a clear opening, paragraphs in a sensible order, linking words, a proper ending?
Are the sentences correct and varied? Is the punctuation correct and wide-ranging? Are the tenses consistent?
Are words spelt correctly, including longer and more ambitious words?
has few ideas, may wander off the task, ignores the reader
covers the task with some detail, mostly suits the purpose
covers every point in detail, clearly fits the purpose and reader, and sounds like a real text of that type
uses simple, repeated words (good, nice, big)
uses precise, varied words chosen for effect (delighted, determined, enormous)
is one long block or has paragraphs in a random order
has paragraphs and some linking words
has a strong opening, well-ordered paragraphs, smooth links between them and a satisfying ending
has many errors, run-on sentences and only full stops
is mostly correct, with a few types of punctuation
is accurate, mixes short and long sentences, and uses a wide range of punctuation correctly
has many errors, even with common words
spells almost everything correctly, including longer words

blocks.title: Rules that can cost you marks before your writing is even judged
items: 20 words or fewer = 0 marks for the whole task.
21 to 60 words = no more than 7 marks out of 25, however good the writing is. Always write a full answer.
Writing the wrong text type (for example, a story when a report was asked for) means Creation of texts can get only 1 mark and Structure is limited too.
Your plan is not marked, but a good plan raises the marks of everything else.

blocks.title: How long should my answer be?
blocks.text: Aim for about 250–350 words. With about 30 minutes for writing, that is long enough to develop every point, short enough to finish and check. Quality matters more than length.
2. Writing purposes vs writing formats

Almost every writing task asks you to do two separate jobs at once. **Purpose** is *why* you are writing: the effect you want on the reader (to inform, explain, describe, persuade, argue, recount, instruct or entertain). **Format** is *how the writing is packaged*: its layout, such as a letter, an email, a diary entry, a report, a leaflet or a review.

Students lose marks because they mix these two up. Some think a format always has one fixed purpose ("a report can only inform"). Others think every task must have a format, even when none is named. In fact, **one purpose can be written in many formats, and one format can serve many purposes.**

rows: Why am I writing this? What do I want my reader to think, feel or do?
What should this look like on the page?
The intention in the task (convince, explain, describe, recount…)
Only what the task names directly. Never guessed.
If the task does not say
You still work it out from the wording
Write normal, well-paragraphed writing with no special layout
Can be more than one (a main purpose and a second one)

blocks.title: The Golden Rule (from the teacher's book)
blocks.text: A piece of writing can have more than one purpose, but it can only ever have ONE format. A format's special features (a greeting, an address, a headline, a date line, a sign-off) are used ONLY when the task names that format. If no format is named, do not invent one. Write clear, organised paragraphs that do the job the task asks for.

**Example 1:** *"The old playground in your town is going to be closed. Write to convince people that it should stay open."* The purpose is to **persuade** (the word *convince* tells you). No format is named: there is no "letter", "article" or "speech". So you write normal persuasive paragraphs with a title, and **no** greeting, address or headline.

**Example 2:** *"Write a letter to your local council explaining why the playground should stay open."* The purpose is the same (persuade), but now the format is named: a **letter**. Now, and only now, you use letter layout: greeting, organised paragraphs and a proper sign-off.
The purposes you need to know

rows: Gives facts so the reader understands something
inform, tell readers about, report on
Shows how or why something happens
Paints a picture with the senses
describe, what it was like, create a picture
Makes the reader agree or act (one side only)
Looks at both sides, then gives a conclusion
discuss, for and against, both sides
Retells real events in time order
recount, write about a time when, what happened
Tells the reader how to do something step by step
Keeps the reader interested and amused

blocks.title: Main purpose first
blocks.text: Many tasks mix purposes. A review informs AND persuades. A diary recounts AND describes feelings. Always ask: "What is the MAIN effect I want on my reader?" That is your main purpose, and it decides most of your language choices.
The formats you need to know

headers: Key layout features (use only when this format is named)
rows: greeting (Dear…,), paragraphs, sign-off (Yours sincerely, / Best wishes,), your name
subject line, greeting, short paragraphs, sign-off
date, Dear Diary, first person, informal, feelings and reflection
title, time order, past tense, time connectives, reflection at the end
title, first person, sub-headings (optional), past tense, reflection
title, third person, sub-headings, dates, quotation
headline, who/what/where/when/why opening, quotations, third person
title of the thing reviewed, description, opinion, recommendation, rating
heading, sub-headings, bullet points, short sections, contact details
title, 'You will need' list, numbered steps, imperative verbs
headline, engaging opening, paragraphs (sub-headings in longer pieces)

blocks.text: Same purpose, different formats

rows: article, letter (only if named), leaflet, speech, advert, normal persuasive writing
report, leaflet, article, email, biography, information text
recount, diary entry, autobiography, letter or email to a friend, blog

blocks.title: قاعدة ذهبية: الهدف والشكل
blocks.text: الهدف (Purpose) هو لماذا تكتب: تقنع؟ تخبر؟ تحكي ما حدث؟ أما الشكل (Format) فهو شكل الكتابة على الورقة: خطاب، إيميل، مذكرات، تقرير. إذا لم يذكر السؤال الشكل بالاسم، لا تخترع شكلاً: لا تكتب Dear ولا عنواناً صحفياً، بل اكتب فقرات منظمة بعنوان بسيط تحقق الهدف. وإذا ذكره، فالتزم بكل ملامحه.

items.q: "Your school is having a 'Kindness Week'. Write to encourage other pupils to take part." Purpose? Format?
items.a: Purpose: persuade (the word 'encourage'). Format: none named, so write normal persuasive paragraphs with a title. No greeting, no headline.

items.q: "Write a diary entry about the first day of the summer holidays." Purpose? Format?
items.a: Purpose: recount and express feelings. Format: diary entry (named), so use the date, Dear Diary, first person and an informal, personal tone.

items.q: "Write a review of a book you enjoyed for the school library's website." Purpose? Format?
items.a: Main purpose: inform AND persuade (tell readers about the book and recommend it). Format: review (named), so name the book, describe it without spoiling the ending, give your opinion and a recommendation or rating.

items.q: "Write about a time when you helped someone." Purpose? Format?
items.a: Purpose: recount. Format: none named, so write a normal recount: title, events in time order, feelings and a reflection. Do not add Dear Diary or a date line.

items.q: "Explain to a younger pupil how to look after a class pet." Purpose? Format?
items.a: Purpose: explain / instruct. Format: none named, so write clear, organised paragraphs (you may use steps). Do not turn it into a letter.

blocks.text: 3. Formal vs informal language (register)

**Register** means how formal or informal your language is. You choose it by asking three questions: **Who** is reading? **Why** am I writing? **What format** has the task named? A letter to a headteacher needs a different register from a diary entry. Choosing the wrong register is one of the easiest ways to lose marks in Creation of texts and Vocabulary, even when your ideas are excellent.

rows: Not used: cannot, do not, I am
Can be short, chatty, with questions and exclamations
formal letter, report, biography, news report, information text
diary, informal letter or email, some blogs

blocks.text: **Formal:** *"I would be grateful if you could provide more benches in the park."*  **Informal:** *"Can you put some more benches in the park? That'd be great!"* Both say the same thing. Only one suits a letter to the council.

items: I received your letter on Monday.
I would like to request a meeting.
I am writing to inform you that…
The event will begin at nine o'clock.
Tickets can be purchased at the gate.
There has been a significant improvement.
The path is in poor condition.

groups.title: Formal openers and linking phrases
items: In my opinion, … / I firmly believe that…
Thank you for taking the time to read this.

items.q: Rewrite formally: "Can you help me with my project?"
items.a: "Could you please assist me with my project?" (or "I would be grateful if you could help me with my project.")

items.q: Rewrite formally: "I can't come to the match because I'm sick."
items.a: "I am unable to attend the match because I am ill." (no contractions, more precise words)

items.q: Rewrite formally: "There's loads of rubbish in the park and it's really bad."
items.a: "There is a large amount of litter in the park, and the situation is very poor."

items.q: Rewrite formally: "Sorry, I messed up the poster."
items.a: "I apologise for the mistakes I made on the poster."

items.q: Which register for: (a) a diary entry about your birthday, (b) a report for the headteacher about the school trip?
items.a: (a) Informal: it is private and personal. (b) Formal: the reader is a person in authority and the purpose is to inform.

blocks.text: 4. How to read a Paper 1 writing task

Checkpoint tasks rarely say "Write a persuasive article". Usually you get a short **situation** (a scenario), an **instruction**, and then some **bullet points** to help you. Read every part slowly and underline the key words before you plan.

blocks.title: An exam-style task (original)
blocks.text: Your school wants to start a new club that meets once a week after school. The headteacher has asked pupils to suggest ideas. Write to persuade the headteacher that your idea is the best one. Consider: • what the club would do • who could join • how it would help pupils • what equipment or help it would need.

rows: A new weekly club. The headteacher wants ideas.
The AUDIENCE and so the REGISTER
No format named, so normal persuasive paragraphs with a title
4 points: what it does, who joins, how it helps, what it needs

blocks.title: 'Consider' vs 'Think' (the teacher's rule)
items: **Consider** = you MUST use at least three of the bullet points in your writing. You may add your own ideas as well.
**Think about** = the bullets are only suggestions. You may use them or your own ideas.
Safest habit for both: use every bullet, one paragraph each. You can never lose marks for covering them all.

blocks.text: 5. The G.A.A.P. technique

Before you write a single sentence, spend the first few minutes breaking the task down with **G.A.A.P.**: **G**enre, **A**udience, **A**rea of content, **P**urpose. (Some people call it GAP, but it has four parts, not three.) Each letter matches something the examiner checks, so G.A.A.P. is not extra work: it protects your marks.
G = Genre (two parts: layout + topic)

items: **Layout:** what kind of text must you produce? If a format is named, list its features (for a diary: date, Dear Diary, first person, feelings). If no format is named, write normal paragraphs with a title.
**Topic:** what exactly is the task about? Be precise. Not "school" but "a new after-school club". Not "the environment" but "litter in the school playground".

blocks.text: A = Audience

items: Where will it be read? (a school magazine, a newspaper, a letter to the headteacher, a private diary, a class display)
Who exactly will read it? (children your age, parents, a teacher, the council, yourself)
So which register? Formal for people in authority and the public. Informal for friends, family and your diary.

blocks.text: A = Area of content

items: Underline every point the task gives you.
Use all of them. Do not skip the hardest one: missing a point costs Creation of texts marks.
Develop each point. One sentence per point is never enough. Add an example, a reason, a feeling or a detail.

blocks.text: P = Purpose

rows: 'you', questions to the reader, strong adjectives, a personal example, a call to action at the end
facts, numbers and dates, clear sub-headings, a neutral tone, third person
reasons and results: because, so, as a result, this means that
time order, past tense, time connectives, feelings, a reflection at the end
both sides, 'On the one hand… On the other hand…', a balanced conclusion
No format named → normal persuasive writing with a title. No 'Dear Headteacher'.
My idea for a new weekly after-school club (for example, a chess club)
The headteacher → formal, polite, no contractions, no slang
'Consider' → use at least 3 bullets. Use all 4: what it does · who can join · how it helps · what it needs
Persuade → questions to the reader, strong reasons, examples, a confident ending
Is it the right text type with the right features?
Creation of texts, Structure of texts
Is everything relevant? Are all points covered and developed?
Are the tone and words right for the reader?
Creation of texts, Vocabulary and language
Are the right techniques used for the right reason?
Creation of texts, Vocabulary and language

blocks.title: طريقة G.A.A.P. في أول خمس دقائق
items: G = نوع الكتابة وشكلها + الموضوع بالضبط.
A = مَن القارئ؟ مدير المدرسة = لغة رسمية، صديق أو مذكراتك = لغة غير رسمية.
A = ضع خطاً تحت كل نقطة في السؤال واكتب عن كل نقطة بالتفصيل (مثال، سبب، شعور).
P = الهدف: إقناع؟ إخبار؟ حكي ما حدث؟ الهدف يحدد الأدوات التي تستخدمها.
Consider = يجب أن تستخدم ثلاث نقاط على الأقل. Think = النقاط مجرد اقتراح.

items.q: Do a G.A.A.P. for: "Write a recount of a school trip for the class blog. Think about: where you went, what you did, the best moment, what you learned."
items.a: G: recount for a blog → title, past tense, time order, first person (format named: blog, so a friendly, lively tone). Topic: one school trip. A: classmates and parents reading the blog → friendly but correct, little slang. A: four bullets ('Think about' = suggestions, but use them all). P: recount and entertain → time connectives, feelings, vivid details, a reflection at the end.

items.q: Do a G.A.A.P. for: "Write a letter to the headteacher asking for longer lunch breaks. Consider: why pupils need more time, what they could do with it, how lessons would not suffer."
items.a: G: formal letter (named) → Dear…, clear reason in paragraph 1, Yours sincerely, full name. Topic: longer lunch breaks. A: headteacher → formal, polite, no contractions. A: 'Consider' → use at least three points (there are three, so use them all). P: persuade politely → reasons, examples, answering the worry about lessons, a polite request at the end.

items.q: Do a G.A.A.P. for: "Write a biography of a person from your town that you admire, for a school booklet."
items.a: G: biography (named) → title, third person, past tense, sub-headings, dates, a quotation. Topic: one admired local person. A: readers of a school booklet (pupils, parents, teachers) → formal and clear. A: no bullets given, so use the biography structure (early life, education, work, achievements). P: inform (and show admiration) → facts, dates, achievements, why they will be remembered.

blocks.text: 6. The 5-minute plan

Your plan is not marked, so keep it short: key words only, never full sentences. A good plan takes about five minutes and saves you from forgetting a bullet, repeating yourself or running out of ideas halfway.

rows: Read the task twice. Underline the purpose word, the reader, any format word and every bullet.
Write G.A.A.P. in one line at the top of the planning space.
Draw boxes: one for each paragraph. Put each bullet into its own box with 2 or 3 key words (an example, a feeling, a detail).
Choose your title, your first sentence and your last idea (an ending that links back to the start). Pick two ambitious words to use.

blocks.text: **Example plan for the club task:** Title: *Checkmate! Why We Need a Chess Club.* P1 Hook: question → "What if one hour a week could make us better thinkers?" + my idea. P2 What it does: learn rules, puzzles, mini-tournament, older pupils teach younger. P3 Who joins: Years 4 to 6, beginners welcome, no cost. P4 How it helps: concentration, patience, friendship, maths. P5 What it needs: 10 chess sets, one classroom, a teacher to supervise, parents could donate sets. P6 Ending: "Give us one hour and we will give you a school of thinkers."
7. Timing inside your 30 minutes

rows: Write (about 4 minutes per paragraph for a five-paragraph answer)
Check: every bullet covered? Paragraphs clear? Full stops and capital letters? Tenses? Spelling of your ambitious words?

blocks.text: If you finish the reading section early, give the extra minutes to the writing. If you are running out of time, write a short final paragraph rather than leaving the piece without an ending: an ending is part of the Structure mark.
8. Paragraphing

A paragraph is a group of sentences about ONE main idea. In Checkpoint, good paragraphs earn marks in **Structure of texts** (7 marks): the examiner wants a clear opening, a body in a sensible order and an ending. Start a new paragraph when you change **topic, time, place or person speaking**.

rows: from 'what the club does' to 'who can join'
a new person speaks (in direct speech)

blocks.text: The shape of a strong body paragraph

rows: Tells the reader what this paragraph is about
Chess would also help pupils in their lessons.
Gives an example, a fact or a description
Every move needs you to think three steps ahead, just like a hard maths problem.
This means pupils would learn to slow down and check their answers.
Leads to the next idea or back to the purpose
Of course, a club like this needs a few simple things to begin.

blocks.title: Weak vs strong
blocks.text: Weak: "Chess is good. It helps you think. It is fun." (three short facts, no development) Strong: "Chess would also help pupils in their lessons. Every move needs you to think three steps ahead, just like a difficult maths problem. As a result, players learn to slow down, plan and check, which are skills every teacher wants."
9. Strong sample (no format named)
Notice: this task names **no format**, so the answer has a title and paragraphs, with no greeting, no headline and no sign-off. Every bullet has its own paragraph.

blocks.title: Sample: 'Let's Grow Something Together' (persuasive, no format named)
blocks.task: Your school is starting a gardening club on the empty roof of the school building. Some pupils think it will be boring. Write to convince pupils in Years 5 and 6 to join the club. Think about: • what members will do • how gardening can help your health and mood • what the school will gain • why it is worth giving up one break a week.
text: What if one break a week could give you fresh air, new friends and a basket of tomatoes that you grew yourself? That is exactly what our new rooftop gardening club offers, and I believe every pupil in Years 5 and 6 should join it.

First of all, members will not just water a few plants and go home. Every Tuesday, we will plant seeds, build wooden boxes for herbs and keep a growth diary for each plant. Mr Karim, our science teacher, will show us how to turn fruit peel from the canteen into compost. In other words, the club is a science lesson that you can touch, smell and even eat.

Gardening is also wonderful for your health and your mood. After hours of sitting at a desk, your body needs to move: digging, carrying and planting keep you active without you even noticing. Many people find that time with plants makes them feel calmer, too. Imagine stepping onto the roof after a difficult maths test. The sun is warm, the mint smells sweet and your worries slowly melt away.

Our school will gain a great deal as well. The roof is grey and empty at the moment; soon it could be green and full of life. The vegetables we grow could be cooked in the canteen, and our flowers could brighten the entrance for visitors. Wouldn't you feel proud to point at them and say, 'I helped to make that'?

Some of you might say, 'But break time is for playing!' I understand, because I love football as much as anyone. However, the club takes only one break a week, so you will still have four left. What you get in return is worth far more: a new skill, new friends and the joy of watching something grow because of you.
So, do not wait for someone else to take your place. Put your name on the list outside the library before Friday. Join the gardening club and help our school bloom.
blocks.marks: Strong answer — Creation 5/5 · Vocabulary 3/3 · Structure 7/7 · Grammar & punctuation 7/7 · Spelling 3/3
notes: Format decision: no format was named, so there is a title and paragraphs only (no 'Dear…', no headline, no sign-off). This is the correct choice and protects Creation and Structure marks.

Creation of texts 5/5: all four bullets are covered and developed, one paragraph each: what members do (P2), health and mood (P3), what the school gains (P4), why it is worth one break (P5). The writer talks directly to the reader ('you', 'Imagine', 'Wouldn't you…?') all the way through and ends with a clear call to action.

Persuasive tools: an opening question, a list of three ('fresh air, new friends and a basket of tomatoes'), a teacher's support as evidence, a picture for the reader to imagine (P3), an objection answered ('But break time is for playing!') and imperatives at the end ('Put your name…', 'Join…').
Vocabulary and language 3/3: precise, lively words ('compost', 'brighten', 'melt away', 'bloom'). The final word 'bloom' links back to gardening and to the title.

Structure of texts 7/7: a hook and clear position in P1. Topic sentences start each body paragraph ('First of all…', 'Gardening is also…', 'Our school will gain…', 'Some of you might say…'). The ending repeats the call to action and links back to the title.

Grammar and punctuation 7/7: a mix of questions, short and long sentences. A colon to explain (P3) and a colon before a list (P5). A semicolon joining two closely related sentences (P4). A pair of commas for extra information ('Mr Karim, our science teacher,'). Apostrophes ('Let's', 'Wouldn't') and correct quotation marks.
Word structure (spelling) 3/3: longer words spelt correctly: 'canteen', 'compost', 'difficult', 'brighten', 'visitors', 'gardening'.
Length: inside the 250–350 range a Year 6 pupil can write and check in about 30 minutes.

blocks.text: 10. Common mistakes

items: Starting to write without reading the whole task, then missing a bullet point.
Inventing a format: writing 'Dear Headteacher' or a newspaper headline when the task never asked for a letter or a report.
Mixing two formats, for example starting like a letter and ending like a diary.
Using the wrong register: slang and 'gonna' in a formal piece, or stiff, formal words in a diary.
One long block of writing with no paragraphs.
Mentioning each bullet in one short sentence instead of developing it with details and examples.
No ending: the piece just stops when time runs out.
Writing too little: 60 words or fewer caps your mark at 7 out of 25.

blocks.title: Before-you-write checklist
items: I have underlined the purpose word, the reader, any format word and every bullet.
I have done G.A.A.P. in one line.
I know whether a format is named. If not, I will write a title and normal paragraphs.
I have chosen formal or informal language and I will keep it the same to the end.
My plan has one box per paragraph, with every bullet in a box.
I know my first sentence and my last idea.
I have chosen two or three ambitious words to use.
I will leave 5 minutes to check punctuation, tenses and spelling.

blocks.title: أهم أخطاء الطلاب وكيف تتجنبها
blocks.text: اقرأ السؤال كله قبل أن تكتب، وضع خطاً تحت كل نقطة. لا تخترع شكلاً لم يُطلب (لا تكتب Dear إلا إذا طُلب خطاب). اكتب فقرة لكل نقطة واشرحها بمثال أو سبب أو شعور. اجعل لكتابتك بداية قوية ونهاية واضحة، واترك خمس دقائق في النهاية للمراجعة. وتذكّر: إذا كتبت 60 كلمة أو أقل فلن تحصل على أكثر من 7 من 25.
11. Practice task

items.q: Practice: "Many children spend most of their weekends indoors. Write to persuade pupils of your age to spend more time outdoors at the weekend. Consider: • what they could do outside • how it helps their bodies and minds • how families can join in • what they miss by staying inside." Write a short plan (G.A.A.P. + paragraph boxes).
items.a: G: no format named → title + persuasive paragraphs, no greeting. Topic: spending weekends outdoors. A: pupils my age → friendly but correct, direct 'you'. A: 'Consider' → at least 3 bullets, use all 4. P: persuade → question opening, examples, imagine-picture, objection answered, call to action. Title: 'Switch Off, Step Out'. P1 Hook: 'When did you last feel grass under your feet?' + position. P2 What to do: cycling, football, planting, a picnic in the park, flying a kite. P3 Body and mind: stronger, better sleep, calmer, less screen tiredness. P4 Families: Friday walk by the Nile, grandparents' garden, family match. P5 What you miss: sunsets, real friends, adventures. Answer the objection 'it's too hot': go early morning or evening. P6 Call to action: 'This weekend, choose one hour outside.' Link back to the title.
